implementation_notes: Swift extensions add methods to any type without touching its source, and protocol extensions provide the implementation once for every conforming type - which is the servant plus its capability interface expressed in one language feature (extension Movable { mutating func moveTo(...) }). Conforming types can also be made after the fact (retroactive conformance), so unrelated or third-party types join the group by declaring conformance in an extension. The implementation is statically dispatched unless the requirement is declared in the protocol itself, and the classic servant object is still the right choice when the behaviour carries configuration or must be substituted in tests.
pitfalls: A method implemented only in a protocol extension is dispatched statically: a conforming type may declare an identical member that shadows it, and callers that see the concrete type run different code than callers that see the protocol - declare a requirement in the protocol when overriding must work.

Extensions cannot add stored properties or deinitialisers, so a servant that needs per-object state must be a separate object; retroactive conformance of a foreign type to your protocol is process-global and can conflict between modules.
sources: The Swift Programming Language, Extensions - adding methods to types whose source you do not have (retroactive modelling) and extending protocols to provide implementations; https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/extensions/

The Swift Programming Language, Protocols - protocol extensions provide method/initializer/subscript/computed-property implementations to conforming types, including adding conformance with an extension; https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/protocols/
